result:
No, this wording has real legal risk. Three issues:

1. **"Open and safe for anyone to use in production payment systems"** — MIT is a permissive license, but it explicitly disclaims all warranties ("AS IS," no liability). Conflating "open source" with "safe for production" contradicts the license's own no-warranty language and could be read as a safety/fitness-for-purpose claim you can't back up.

2. **"Fully compliant with PCI security standards"** — this is the big one. PCI DSS compliance isn't something a library declares about itself based on internal testing; it's a certification obtained through formal assessment (QSA audit, SAQ, etc.) of an entire cardholder-data environment, not a codebase in isolation. Saying a library is "PCI compliant" is generally a category error and, if untrue or unverified, could expose you to false-advertising or misrepresentation claims — especially since users of a "payment-validation library" will reasonably rely on this statement.

3. **"Passed all our internal tests"** — fine as a factual statement, but it's doing a lot of work to imply security guarantees ("therefore safe," "therefore compliant") that don't follow from internal testing alone.

Suggested direction (not final language — flag this back to legal/marketing together): state facts you can actually substantiate — license type, what internal testing covered, and that PCI DSS compliance is the responsibility of the merchant/integrator's environment as a whole, not something this library confers. Something like separating "MIT licensed" (factual) from testing scope (factual, specific) and dropping the PCI claim entirely unless you have an actual assessment to point to.

Want me to draft revised README wording for you to run past legal, or just flag the concerns as-is?
